column2: Then Vishnu went to Varuna, lord of the waters, Mahashani's father-in-law; reaching Varuna, Keshava told him of Indra's defeat:
You must act so that Purandara comes back. At Vishnu's word the lord of the waters quickly went, O sage,
to valiant Mahashani, son of Hiranya and his daughter's husband; the lord Varuna was greatly honoured by his son-in-law.
The Daitya then humbly asked his father-in-law why he had come, and Varuna told the Daitya the reason for his coming:

Give me Indra, O mighty-armed one, whom you conquered long ago — the lord of the gods, bound and kept in Rasatala, my friend.
brahmapuran:129:28	He is always to be honoured by us; give him to me, O slayer of foes. To release an enemy after binding him brings great fame among the good.
Saying "So be it," the lord of the Daityas reluctantly gave Indra, Shachi's husband, together with his elephant, to Varuna.
Shining brilliantly amid the Daityas, in the presence of the lord of the waters, Mahashani honoured Maghavan with great ceremony and then said to him:

Who has made you Indra today? Who gave you such valour, that you boast so much? You are harassed by enemies in battle, and still you are Indra — how strange!
brahmapuran:129:32	When some woman is held captive by a man, it is fitting that her husband sets her free; women are dependent and ruled by men — and you, good Shakra, are supposed to be a man!
brahmapuran:129:33	I bound you in battle along with your mount. Where was your weapon then, the thunderbolt of unbounded power? The wish-granting jewel, the Nandana grove, those women, fame and strength — the enjoyments of the king of the gods —
brahmapuran:129:34	that alone is life which is a treasury of fame, and that alone is death which is opposed to fame. Knowing this, Shakra, how is it that, having won release through the lord of the waters, you feel no shame?
brahmapuran:129:35	Dwelling in heaven, surrounded by all the gods, fanned by your beloved and praised by the Apsaras — surely shame itself is afraid of you, I think.
brahmapuran:129:36	'You are the slayer of Vritra and of Namuchi, breaker of cities, splitter of mountains, thunderbolt-armed' — so the gods worship you; therefore, O Jishnu, give all this up.
brahmapuran:129:37	Those who go on living and mixing with people even after suffering disgrace at the hands of enemies — how did the lotus-born creator of such as you not have his heart break?
Having said this, the lord of the Daityas handed Indra over to the great-souled Varuna and spoke these words again:

From today let this Indra be the disciple, and Varuna, my father-in-law, through whom you have gained release, be the teacher, O Vasava.
brahmapuran:129:40	You must behave as a servant toward Varuna; otherwise I will bind you again and throw you into Rasatala.
Having rebuked Shakra thus, laughing again and again, he said, "Go, go," and took leave of Varuna.
Reaching his own abode, stained with shame, Indra told Pauloma's daughter everything about his defeat by the enemy.
Thus was I spoken to and treated by the enemy, fair-faced one; tell me, fortunate one, how I may find relief.

I know the origin of the Danavas, Shakra, their magic, their defeat, their boons and their death, O slayer of Bala.
brahmapuran:129:45	So listen: I will tell you everything by which his death or defeat may come about, for your satisfaction.
brahmapuran:129:46	The heroic son of Hiranya is the mighty son of my paternal uncle, so he is my brother, and he is proud from a boon.
brahmapuran:129:47	He pleased Brahma with austerity and discipline and gained such strength; what is not achieved by austerity?
brahmapuran:129:48	So you should feel neither distress nor wonder at all. Listen to what must be done here, as it has come down in due order.
Having said this, Pauloma's daughter humbly spoke to Indra:

Nothing is impossible for austerity, nothing impossible for sacrificial rites, and nothing impossible through devotion to Vishnu, lord of the worlds, and to Hara.
brahmapuran:129:51	And I have heard this excellent saying, beloved: only women truly know the nature of women, O lord of the gods.
brahmapuran:129:52	Likewise nothing is impossible for the earth and the waters, O lord, since austerity and sacrifice and the like come about through them alone.
brahmapuran:129:53	Even among these, you should go to the land that is a tirtha; worshipping Vishnu and Shiva there, you will obtain all your desires.
brahmapuran:129:54	I have also heard this: women who are faithful to their husbands know everything, and by them the moving and unmoving world is upheld.
brahmapuran:129:55	The essence of the earth is the Dandaka forest in its midst; there flows the Ganga, upholder of the world. Worship the Lord there, O lord,
brahmapuran:129:56	or Vishnu, lord of the worlds, the all-pervading one who removes the pain of the wretched and afflicted. For helpless men here, sinking in the ocean of sorrow,
brahmapuran:129:57	there is no other refuge anywhere but Hara, Hari or the Ganga. So with every effort, and with a collected mind, please them
brahmapuran:129:58	with devotion, hymns and austerity; do this together with me. Then you will obtain the welfare that comes from the grace of Isha and Vishnu.
brahmapuran:129:59	A rite done without understanding gives the doer a single measure of fruit; done with understanding it becomes a hundredfold, and done with one's wife it is imperishable.
brahmapuran:129:60	In all a man's undertakings the wife alone is his helper here; without her even small tasks do not succeed.
brahmapuran:129:61	A rite performed by one person alone yields half the fruit; performed with his wife, O lord, a man gains the full.
brahmapuran:129:62	So it is well known from the Veda that 'the wife is half.' It is heard that in the Dandaka forest flows the Gautami, best of rivers,
brahmapuran:129:63	which quells all sin and grants every wish. So go there with me and perform merit of great fruit.
brahmapuran:129:64	Then, having slain your enemies in battle, you will attain great happiness.
Saying "So be it," Shatakratu, with his teacher and his wife, went to the Ganga, upholder of the world, famed as the Gautami.
Hari went gladly to her in the midst of the Dandaka forest and resolved to perform austerity for Shambhu, the God of gods.
First bowing to the Ganga and bathing, with joined palms and taking Shiva as his sole refuge, he then spoke this hymn:

He who by his own maya creates, sustains and devours this whole world of moving and unmoving things yet is not attached to it — the one, independent, non-dual consciousness whose nature is bliss — may that Pinaka-bearer be gracious to us.
brahmapuran:129:69	He whose truth not even Sanaka and the others, knowers of the secret of Vedanta, can know — may that lord of Parvati, giver of all desires, enemy of Andhaka, be gracious to me.
brahmapuran:129:70	The self-born Lord, having created Brahma, saw that his head was fearsome; he cut it off with his fingernails and flung it away as it clung to his nail, and from it arose the triad of ills:
brahmapuran:129:71	sin and poverty, then greed and begging, delusion and calamity, and from these endless others, powerful, the very form of worldly sorrow; this whole world became pervaded by them.
brahmapuran:129:72	Seeing all this, the lord of the gods, alarmed, said to the Goddess: 'The world is going to ruin; protect it, O Queen of the worlds, Mother of the worlds, Uma, giver of refuge, fortunate and most auspicious one.
brahmapuran:129:73	Foundation of the world, giver of boons, victory to you! You are enjoyment, samadhi and supreme liberation; Svaha, Svadha, well-being, beginningless perfection, speech, intellect and blessing — you are unageing and immortal.
brahmapuran:129:74	In the form of knowledge and the rest you protect the three worlds at my command; by you alone the three worlds are created, for this manifold wonder arises from Prakriti alone.'
brahmapuran:129:75	Addressed thus by Hara, his beloved became absorbed in embraces and tender talk; weary, closely joined in half of Bhava's body, she flicked drops of sweat from her fingertips.
brahmapuran:129:76	From that there arose first Dharma, then Lakshmi, then charity, then good rain, goodness, the fertile earth, lakes, grains, flowers and fruits,
brahmapuran:129:77	things of good fortune, beauty, fine dress, adornments, great medicines, dances, songs, nectar, the Puranas, Shruti and Smriti, statecraft, food and drink,
brahmapuran:129:78	weapons, sciences, household goods, missiles, tirthas and forests, sacrifices and works of public merit, auspicious things, vehicles, bright ornaments and seats.
brahmapuran:129:79	From contact with Bhava's body, from laughter, sweat, tender talk and the ways of intimacy, the whole world of moving and unmoving beings arose, free from sin, O Goddess;
brahmapuran:129:80	and abundant happiness and good ever shine forth from your being, O Goddess. So protect me, Mother of the world, foremost of the worlds, for I am afraid of dangers.
brahmapuran:129:81	Some are bewildered by reasonings, others are absorbed in it; I praise that beautiful form, the non-duality of Shiva and Shakti.
As he praised thus, Shiva appeared before him:
What wish do you choose, Hari? Tell me your aim.

I had a mighty enemy, baleful to look upon like Saturn; bound by him, I was taken to the netherworld and humiliated in many ways,
brahmapuran:129:85	and pierced as well by arrows of words; this effort is for his slaying. For that purpose, O Lord of the worlds, by which I may conquer my enemy, O lord,
brahmapuran:129:86	give me that very strength, and whatever else destroys enemies. When he who caused my defeat is destroyed, I shall count myself reborn — that is the boon I prize for fame, victory and glory.
Shiva said to Shakra: "Your enemy will not meet his death through me alone; so you must also worship Vishnu, the imperishable Hari,
the god Janardana, together with Pauloma's daughter — Narayana, sole refuge of the three worlds — with single-minded devotion.
Then you will obtain what you desire from him and from me as well, Hari." And the blessed Maheshvara, the first creator, spoke again:

The sages know that mantra practice, austerity or the practice of yoga at any confluence whatever brings success.
brahmapuran:129:91	How much more at the confluence of the Gautami and the Phena, O brahmin! Or in mountain caves, or at the meeting of rivers,
brahmapuran:129:92	one becomes a true brahmin through a mind fixed on Mukunda's feet. On the southern bank of the Ganga lives Apastamba, lord of sages;
brahmapuran:129:93	I too was pleased with him, O slayer of Bala. With him and with your wife, please the bearer of the mace.
Together with Apastamba, on the southern bank of the Ganga, he praised the god with self-restraint, having bathed at the holy confluence
of the Phena and the Ganga; there he then pleased the god Janardana with various Vedic mantras and with austerity.
Then Vishnu was pleased and said, "What shall I give?" Lord Hari (Indra) said, "Give me a slayer of my enemy."
Janardana said to him, "Know that it is given." There, by the grace of Shiva, the Ganga and Vishnu,
a man was born from the water, bearing the form of both Shiva and Vishnu, holding discus and trident; he went to Rasatala
and slew the Daitya Mahashani, Indra's enemy. That water-born Abjaka, who is Vrishakapi, became Indra's friend.
Even while in heaven Indra always followed Vrishakapi. Seeing him attached to another, Shachi grew angry out of love; soothing her, Shatamanyu said with a smile:

O Indrani, I have no refuge except my friend Vrishakapi, whose water and oblation are always dear to Agni.
brahmapuran:129:102	I will not go elsewhere, my love; I swear by your body. So you should not speak to me with suspicion of another, passionate one.
brahmapuran:129:103	You are my beloved, faithful to your husband, my helper in dharma and counsel, a mother, of noble family; who else but you is dear to me?
brahmapuran:129:104	On your advice I came to the Ganga, the great river, and by the grace of Vishnu, God of gods, wielder of the discus,
brahmapuran:129:105	and by the grace of the god Shiva, and through my water-born friend Vrishakapi, the world-famed Abjaka,
brahmapuran:129:106	I have crossed beyond sorrow, fortunate one; from now on I am Indra, unshaken. What cannot be achieved where the wife follows her husband's mind?
brahmapuran:129:107	Even liberation is not hard to gain there, let alone wealth and the other two aims, auspicious one. The wife alone is the supreme friend, seeking one's good in both worlds.
brahmapuran:129:108	If she is of good family, sweet-spoken, faithful, beautiful, rich in virtues, and the same in prosperity and adversity, what in the three worlds is impossible with her?
brahmapuran:129:109	So through your wisdom, beloved, this good has come to me; from now on what you say shall be done — I have no other course.
brahmapuran:129:110	For the next world and for dharma there is nothing like a good son; and for a man in distress here there is no medicine like a wife.
brahmapuran:129:111	For reaching the highest good and for release from sin there is nothing like the Ganga; hear something more, fair-faced one:
brahmapuran:129:112	for gaining dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation and for release from sin, there is nothing here that liberates like knowing that Shiva and Vishnu are not different.
brahmapuran:129:113	So through your wisdom, virtuous one, all that was in my mind has been attained by the grace of Shiva, Vishnu and the Ganga.
brahmapuran:129:114	I think my Indra-hood is secure again through the strength of my friend: Vrishakapi, who was born in the waters, is my companion, passionate one,
brahmapuran:129:115	and you are ever my dear friend; nothing is dearer to me. Among tirthas the Gautami Ganga, among gods Hari and Shankara —
brahmapuran:129:116	by their grace I have obtained all I wished; and this tirtha, famed in the three worlds, gives me joy.
brahmapuran:129:117	So I shall ask this of all the gods in turn; let the sages, the Ganga, and Hari and Shankara consent:
brahmapuran:129:118	at Indreshvara and Abjaka on the two banks, O gods, let the god Shankara stand on one side and Janardana on the other —
brahmapuran:129:119	Vishnu Trivikrama himself, purifying the Dandaka forest. And the tirthas that lie between, granting all merit —
brahmapuran:129:120	by merely bathing here may all attain liberation; may the most sinful be freed from sin, and may the righteous
brahmapuran:129:121	attain supreme liberation along with five generations of ancestors on each side. Whatever those here give to supplicants, even the size of a sesame seed,
brahmapuran:129:122	may it be imperishable for the givers, granting desires and liberation. This story of Vishnu and Shambhu brings blessing, fame, long life, health and increase of merit,
brahmapuran:129:123	and, when known, liberation through bathing. Those who hear and recite the greatness of this tirtha
brahmapuran:129:124	shall share in merit, and here itself shall gain the remembrance of Shiva and Vishnu that cuts away the whole mass of sin, which sages who have mastered their senses and minds pray for.
So it shall be, the gods and sages told him. On the northern bank of the Gautami there are tirthas that grant liberation,
served by gods, sages and Siddhas, seven thousand in number; and on the southern bank likewise there are eleven thousand tirthas.
The great sages call Abjaka the heart of the Godavari, the resting place of Isha, Vishnu and Brahma.

He who is present as fire in wood, fragrance in flowers, the tree in its seed, gold in stone, and likewise in all beings — to that Somanatha I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:24	He who in play made this universe, the creator and ordainer of the three worlds, whose form is the universe and who is beyond being and non-being — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:25	Remembering whom an embodied being is untouched by poverty, great curses, disease and the like, and resorting to whom people gain what they desire — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:26	He who in the beginning, considering the dharma of the three Vedas, set Brahma and the others to their tasks, and who thus made his body twofold — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:27	To whom goes every salutation, every oblation purified by mantras and every act of worship; by whom the gods receive the offerings given — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:28	Beyond whom there is nothing more excellent, beyond whom there is nothing subtler, beyond whom there is nothing greater than the great — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:29	By whose command this wondrous universe, of inconceivable form, manifold and vast, moves as if by a single act — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.
brahmapuran:130:30	In whom are glory, lordship over all, the greatness of creator and giver, love, fame, happiness and beginningless dharma — to that Someshvara I go for refuge.

Then the Lord, pleased, spoke to that sage, O Narada; and Apastamba spoke to Shiva for his own sake and for others':
May those who bathe and behold the god, the Lord of the worlds, obtain all their desires. "So be it," Shiva told the sage.
From then on that tirtha has been called Apastamba, able to uproot the dense darkness of beginningless ignorance.
Whoever, keeping his vows, bathes at Gotirtha or Brahmatirtha, bows to Brahma there and also circumambulates the island,
has by that circumambulated the whole earth with its seven continents. Giving a little wealth there to a brahmin,
and reaching that place of divine sacrifice and offering a little into the fire, he obtains in full the fruit of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice.
Whoever recites there even once the Gayatri, mother of the Vedas, has by that studied the Vedas; free from desire, he becomes a vessel of liberation.
Bathing on the southern bank and duly worshipping the goddess Shakti with devotion, one obtains all desires.
Worshipping Shakti, mother of Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesha, who consists of the three Vedas, one obtains all desires and becomes rich in sons and wealth.
The disciplined man who bathes and devotedly beholds the Sun on the southern bank has thereby performed sacrifices with manifold fees.
And whoever bathes on the northern bank of the Ganga, beholds the slayer of Daityas and bows to him, attains the supreme abode of Vishnu.
Whoever, bathed and self-controlled, then beholds Yameshvara worshipped at Yamatirtha soon brings about
imperishable merit for his ancestors, fruitful and increasing fame. By bathing, giving, japa and praise there, even ancestors of wicked deeds attain liberation.
Thus, O Narada, there are eight thousand and three tirthas; bathing and giving at them all bestows imperishable merit.
Remembering them is meritorious and destroys the sins of many births; hearing of them purifies one along with one's ancestors, and reciting them along with one's whole family;
even their great sins are destroyed at my command. Whoever, self-controlled, bathes there, gives a little,
offers rice-balls and the like to the ancestors and bows to these gods, gains wealth, grain, fame, vigour, long life, health and prosperity,
sons, grandsons, a beloved wife and whatever else he desires; never separated from them, glad of heart and greatly honoured by his kin,

having delivered even ancestors dwelling in hell and purified his families, he, surrounded by loved ones, remembers Vishnu and Shiva at the end and then goes to the state of liberation, as the gods declared.
Then, overwhelmed, she became a river. Seeing that, amazed and afraid, I said to her:
Since you, dwelling in Brahma's speech, have spoken falsely, you shall become invisible; you are surely sinful in form.
Learning of this curse, she bowed to those two gods, begging release from the curse, and praised them again and again.
Then the two Gods of gods, worshipped by the thirty, pleased by her entreaty, Hari and Hara, spoke these words with affection:
When you, good lady, join the Ganga, purifier of the world, then your body will be pure again, lovely one.
Saying "So be it," the goddess joined the Ganga — both the Bhagirathi and the Gautami — and then her own body
the goddess regained, O brahmin, which is hard even for the gods to obtain. In the Gautami she is famed by the name Vani, giver of merit;
in the Bhagirathi the same goddess is called Sarasvati. In both places the confluence is famous and worshipped by the world:
the Sarasvati-sangama and the Vani-sangama. The goddess Vani — Vach, Sarasvati — joined with the Gautami.
That tirtha is worshipped everywhere, because there Vach, having worshipped Shiva, the lord of gods, was freed from the curse,
and Brahma, shaking off the fault of speech, returned to his own abode. So, becoming pure there and bathing at that confluence,
and then beholding Vagishvara, one attains liberation by that alone. Whoever performs there some charity, oblation and the like, or rites such as fasting,
at that holy confluence is not born again in worldly existence. There are nineteen hundred tirthas on the two banks, which destroy all the sins accumulated over many births.
He would joyfully tell them the wondrous stories he had heard from Vishnu. When much time had passed in this way, Maudgalya's wife, greatly puzzled, spoke to her husband in private:

Though Vishnu, worshipped by the thirty gods, comes close to you, still we suffer hardship. Why is this?
brahmapuran:136:16	Ask the Lord of the world this, O wise one, when Vishnu comes. At the mere remembrance of him old age, birth, disease and death are destroyed — how much more when he is seen? So ask the Lord of the world.
Saying "So be it" at his beloved's words, Maudgalya worshipped Hari as usual and, humble and with joined palms, asked him:
When you are remembered, O Lord of the world, grief, poverty and sin are destroyed; how then does my misfortune remain when you are seen?

How can liberation come through devotion? For one bent on enjoyment liberation is very hard. If embodied beings do attain liberation, what need is there of anything else?
brahmapuran:136:28	Liberation through devotion is honoured by all; that is what I would wish for, O you who pervade the world.

This is the difference, O brahmin: whatever is given to a brahmin or to supplicants while remembering me becomes imperishable.
brahmapuran:136:30	What one gives without meditating on me yields only its own measure of fruit; it is merely given here and does not serve for enjoyment hereafter.
brahmapuran:136:31	So, O wise one, you must give me some food, or give it to a chief brahmin while dwelling on the bank of the Gautami.
Maudgalya said to Vishnu, "I have nothing to give — nothing else, not even my body, for that has already been offered to you."
Then Vishnu, Lord of the world, quickly said to Garuda, "Bring an ear of grain here; he will offer it to me,
and then he will obtain fitting enjoyments dear to his heart." Hearing his master's command, the king of birds did so.
Maudgalya, keeping his vows, placed the grains in Vishnu's hand. Meanwhile Vishnu said to Vishvakarma:

For as long as seven generations of his family last, O wise one, let his desires be fulfilled — cattle, gold, grain, clothes and ornaments,
brahmapuran:136:37	and whatever adornment in the world delights the mind. All this Maudgalya obtained through the power of Vishnu and the Ganga.
Told by Vishnu, "Go home," Maudgalya went; seeing every kind of prosperity in his hermitage, the sage said:
Ah, the power of giving! Ah, the remembrance of Vishnu! Ah, the power of the Ganga! Who can fathom this greatness?
Maudgalya, with his wife, sons, grandsons, kinsmen and parents, enjoyed pleasures, and obtained both enjoyment and liberation.
From then on that tirtha has been called Maudgalya and Vaishnava; bathing and giving there yields enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever in any way hears of or remembers that tirtha, Vishnu is pleased with him; freed from sins, he becomes happy.
There are eleven thousand tirthas on the two banks, granting every aim through bathing, giving, japa and the like.
Having sent away the priest, best of brahmins, with wealth, saying, "Make gifts diligently to the pilgrims at another tirtha,"
the king acted without the priest knowing anything of his purpose. When that teacher, the great-souled son of Vishvamitra, had gone, the king
sent away all his forces and entered the fire on the bank of the Ganga. The best of kings first said this to the Ganga, the Sun and the gods:
If I have given, if I have offered oblations, if I have protected my subjects, by that truth may that virtuous lady live with my lifespan.
When Sharyati, best of kings, had said this and entered the fire, at that very moment the wife of the king's priest came back to life.
Hearing, to his amazement, that the king had entered the fire, and that his faithful wife, who had died, was alive again,
and that the king had given up his life especially for her sake, the king's teacher considered what he himself should do:
Shall I too enter the fire and go to my beloved's side, or shall I perform austerity here? Then the brahmin resolved:

This I consider my duty and a good deed: I will revive the king, and then go back to my beloved.
brahmapuran:138:32	This will be good for me. Then he praised the Sun: "There is no other god who grants all desires like the Sun.
Salutations to that Sun of boundless radiance, for liberation; to the god made of the Vedic metres, the meaning of Om, salutations to you.
To the formless and the well-formed, to the one of three qualities and three forms, to the cause of preservation, origin and destruction, to the mighty one."
Then the Sun was pleased and said, "Choose a boon."
Give me back the king, O Lord of gods, and my sweet-spoken wife, good sons for myself, and good boons for the king.
Then the Lord of the world restored Sharyati, adorned with jewels, and the wife, along with other boons and complete well-being.
Then the king, with his beloved queen and his delighted priest, went happily to his own country; that tirtha is remembered as auspicious.
There are three thousand excellent tirthas there. From then on that tirtha has been called Bhanutirtha,
also famed as Mritasanjivana and Sharyata, and known as Madhuchchhandasa; its remembrance removes sin, O sage.
Bathing and giving at them yields the fruit of all sacrifices; that Mritasanjivana increases long life and health.
Then the great soul, by the power of his austerity, summoned Tvashtr and said:
I wish for Indra-hood, great one; quickly make the realm of Indra here. If you answer otherwise than as I have said, I will surely burn you to ashes; there is no doubt of this.
At the word of Atri's son, Vishvakarma, the mighty creator of beings, at once made Meru, the city of the gods, the wish-granting trees, the wish-granting creeper and the wish-granting cow;
he made bright, richly decorated mansions adorned with diamonds and the like; he made a Shachi flawless in every limb, like Kama's own pleasure-hall;
in a moment he made the assembly hall Sudharma and charming Apsaras; he made Ucchaihshravas and the elephant, the thunderbolt and other weapons, and all the gods.
Though his beloved tried to stop him, Atri's son made his own wife equal to Shachi; then Atri's son, joined by Atri and others, also made a weapon in the form of the thunderbolt.
Dances, songs and everything seen in Shakra's city he made. Having obtained all this, the great sage was exceedingly delighted.
Who does not long for the things of the senses, pleasing at first sight? Hearing of it, the Daityas and Danavas assembled, and the Rakshasas too, at once filled with anger:
Why has Hari left heaven and come down to earth? Is it for his own pleasure? Then let us go from here to fight the slayer of Vritra.
Then the asuras came and surrounded the son of Atri, encircling the city he had made, called Indra's city.
He who, as soon as he was born, the first and wise, the god, surpassed the gods in power; at whose might heaven and earth trembled, by the greatness of his manliness — he, O people, is Indra.
With this and other hymns Atri's son answered his enemies and praised Hari (Indra):

I am not Hari, nor is Shachi mine; this is not his city, nor that Indra's grove. He alone is Indra, slayer of Vritra, wielder of the thunderbolt, thousand-eyed, splitter of mountains, thunderbolt-armed.
brahmapuran:140:25	I am a brahmin who knows the Veda, surrounded by assemblies of brahmins, dwelling on the bank of the Gautami; through ill fate I did this deed, which brings happiness neither now nor hereafter.
Withdraw this mockery of Indra, son of Atri; then you will be safe, truly, and not otherwise, O best of sages.
Then Atri's son said, "I will do just as you say here, noble ones; by truth I touch the fire."
Having said this to the Daityas, he spoke again to Tvashtr:

Tvashtr, quickly withdraw the realm of Indra you made here to please me, and protect me, a brahmin sage.
brahmapuran:140:30	Give me back my place, my hermitage, the deer and birds, the trees and the water that were there; I have no need of divine things. What comes out of its proper order brings no happiness to the wise.
Saying "So be it," Tvashtr, lord of creatures, then withdrew it, and the Daityas went to their own place, leaving the land free of trouble.
Tvashtr too went to his own place, as if laughing; and Atri's son, with his disciples and his wife,
dwelling on the bank of the Gautami, intent on austerity and surrounded by all, spoke in shame while a great sacrifice was in progress:
Ah, the power of delusion! Even my mind went astray. Did I gain the realm of great Indra? What have I done here?
As the son of Atri spoke thus in shame, the gods said to him:

Give up your shame, O mighty-armed one; you will have the highest fame. Those beings who readily bathe at Atreyatirtha
brahmapuran:140:37	shall become Indras, and by remembering it they shall share in happiness. The wise say there are five thousand tirthas there,
brahmapuran:140:38	celebrated by the names of Indra, Atreya and the Daityas; bathing and giving at them all bestows imperishable merit.
Having said this, the gods departed, and the sage was content.
Then those steadfast ones, O brahmins, go to the abode of Narasimha and sport there joyfully for ten thousand crores of years.
At the end of that they go to the city of Vishnu, frequented by Siddhas, and sport there happily for tens of thousands of years.
Then, O brahmins, those best of adepts go to Brahma's world, and after staying there a long time, many hundreds of crores of years,
those lords of adepts go on to Narayana's city and enjoy various pleasures for crores and arbudas of years.
Afterwards those best of adepts, of divine form and great strength, go to Aniruddha's city, praised by gods and asuras.
There the Vaishnavas remain for fourteen thousand crores of years, free from old age and death.
Afterwards, free from all fever, they go to Pradyumna's city; there those brahmins remain for three hundred lakh crores of years.
Moving at will, joyful, endowed with strength and power, the yogis then go to where the lord Sankarshana dwells.
Having dwelt there a long time and enjoyed pleasures by the thousand, they enter Vasudeva, the formless and stainless,
released into the supreme principle, free from old age and death; having gone there they become liberated, without doubt.
Thus in due order the wise who are devoted to the worship of Vasudeva attain enjoyment and liberation, O tigers among sages.
Since the body is the means to dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation, the wise should protect the body with great care.
Living, a man gains dharma, wealth and happiness, and likewise the highest state of liberation; living, he wins fame — what is there in the world for a dead man?
Hearing his words, Matanga replied with reason:
Good sir, I go honouring truth; I have sworn oaths.
He answered him again: "Why are you so foolish? Have you not heard, good man, what Manu declared?
To protect cows, women and brahmins, at the time of marriage, in lovemaking, when life is in danger, and when all one's wealth is being seized — these five untruths are declared not to be sins.
Strict truthfulness is not required toward women, at a marriage, toward an enemy, against deceit, in loss of wealth, or when one's own life is at stake." Hearing these words, Matanga replied:

Do not speak so, bless you; truth is honoured in all the worlds. By truth is gained whatever happiness there is in the world.
brahmapuran:228:53	By truth the sun shines, by truth the waters have their taste; by truth fire burns, and by truth the wind blows.
brahmapuran:228:54	The attainment of dharma, wealth and pleasure, and the hard-won attainment of liberation, come to men through truth; therefore one should not abandon truth.
brahmapuran:228:55	Truth is the supreme Brahman in the world, truth is the highest in sacrifices, truth leads to heaven; therefore one should not abandon truth.
Having said this, Matanga brushed that excellent man aside and went to where the brahmarakshasa, the killer of living beings, was.
Seeing the outcaste arrive, the brahmarakshasa, eyes wide with astonishment, shook his head and said to him:

Well done, well done, fortunate one, keeper of your word! I do not consider you an outcaste; you bear the marks of truth.
brahmapuran:228:59	By this deed I consider you a brahmin, pure and unfailing. I will say something to you, good sir, grounded in dharma: tell me, what did you do that night in Vishnu's temple?
Matanga said to him, "Listen: I will tell you truly what I did during the night in Vishnu's temple.
Standing below Vishnu's shrine, I kept vigil through the night, singing songs to Vishnu."
The brahmarakshasa said to him, "Tell me, how long have you, devoted one, kept vigil in Vishnu's temple?"
Laughing, he said to him, "For twenty years, O rakshasa, I have kept vigil there on the Ekadashi of every month." Hearing Matanga's words, the brahmarakshasa said:

What I ask of you now, you ought to grant: give me, good man, the merit of one night's vigil.
brahmapuran:228:65	In that way I will release you — I will release you, and not otherwise; I swear it three times by truth, fortunate one. Having said this, he fell silent.
Matanga then said to him, "I have given myself to you, night-roamer; what use are words? Eat me as you please."
The rakshasa said to him again, "Give me the merit of a vigil of two watches, with its singing; you should show compassion."
Matanga said to the rakshasa, "Why say something so pointless? Eat me as you wish; I will not give you the vigil." Hearing Matanga's words, the brahmarakshasa said to him:

What wicked-minded fool would dare look at you, to assail or torment you, protected as you are by your righteous deeds?
brahmapuran:228:70	Toward the wretched, the sin-afflicted, the one deluded by sense objects, the fool tormented by hell, the good are compassionate.
brahmapuran:228:71	So, fortunate one, show me compassion and give me the vigil of a single watch, or else go to your own home.
The outcaste said to him again, "I will not go to my home, nor will I give you in any way the vigil of a watch." Then the brahmarakshasa, laughing, said to the outcaste:
Give me the fruit of the song you sang with delight at the end of the night; save me, lift me out of sin.
When he had said this, Matanga said to him:
What wrong deed did you commit before, by whose fault you were born a brahmarakshasa?
Hearing his words, the brahmarakshasa, burning with sorrow and remembering what he had done, said to Matanga:

Hear who I was before and what I did, by which I fell into this sinful rakshasa birth.
brahmapuran:228:78	I was formerly a brahmin named Somasharma, son of Devasharma, a studious sacrificer.
brahmapuran:228:79	For a certain royal patron, though I was ignorant of the sutras and mantras, eager for the rite and competent only in the work of the sacrificial post,
brahmapuran:228:80	I served as the Agnidhra priest in the sacrifice, driven by greed and delusion. When it was over, out of foolishness and hypocrisy,
brahmapuran:228:81	I began to perform the great twelve-day sacrifice myself; while it was going on, I was seized by colic.
brahmapuran:228:82	When ten nights were complete and the sacrifice still unfinished, at the moment the oblation to Virupaksha was being offered, in the hour of the rakshasas,
brahmapuran:228:83	I died, and by that fault I was born a brahmarakshasa. Foolish, lacking mantras, without the sutras and the accents,
brahmapuran:228:84	not knowing the science of sacrifice, I sacrificed and made others sacrifice; by the ripening of that karma I was born a brahmarakshasa.
brahmapuran:228:85	So lift me out, sunk as I am in the great ocean of sin; you ought to give me the one last song of your vigil.
The outcaste said to him, "If you will give up killing living beings, then I will give you the last song."
Very well, he said, and Matanga then formally gave him the fruit of the song, a vigil of half a muhurta.
When the fruit of the song had been given, the brahmarakshasa bowed to Matanga and went joyfully to Prithudaka, best of tirthas.
There, resolving to fast, he gave up his life, O brahmins, released from being a rakshasa and strengthened by the fruit of the song,
and by the power of Prithudaka he dwelt free of fear in Brahma's world, hard to attain, for ten thousand years.
At its end he was born a brahmin, remembering his past and self-controlled. I will tell you more of his story later, O brahmins.
Now hear from me the rest of Matanga's story. When the rakshasa had gone, the wise and self-controlled one came home,
and recalling that brahmin's history, he grew dispassionate; though pure, he entrusted his wife to his sons and set out to circumambulate the earth.
Starting from Kokamukha as far as the shrine of Skanda, and having seen Skanda, he went to Dharachakra and circumambulated it.
Then, coming to the Vindhya, best of mountains with lofty peaks, he reached the tirtha Papapramochana, O brahmins.
He, born of an outcaste family, took the sin-removing bath; freed from sin, he remembered his many former births.
In a former birth he had been a mendicant, restrained in speech and mind, restrained in body, wise, master of the Vedas and their limbs.
Once, when cows were being driven off from the city by thieves, that mendicant, dusty from his begging round, let them go unhindered.
By that fault of unrighteousness he came to be born an outcaste. Having bathed at Papapramochana, he died on the bank of the Narmada,
and became a foolish but eminent brahmin in Varanasi, O brahmins. When he had lived there thirty years, a Siddha
of strange form was wandering about, endowed with the power of a rosary of yoga. Seeing him, the brahmin greeted him in jest and said:
Greetings, perfected one! Where have you come from?
Addressed thus, and thinking, "I have been recognized," the venerable one replied, "I have come from the world of heaven."
The fool said to the Siddha, "Do you know, in heaven, Urvashi, best of Apsaras, born from Narayana's thigh?"
The Siddha said, "I know her — Urvashi, who holds Shakra's fly-whisk, the chief ornament of heaven, of noble birth."
Then the brahmin, straying from the straight path, said to the Siddha, "Then, friend, kindly carry a message to Urvashi for me,
and tell me whatever she says to you." "Very well," said the Siddha, and the brahmin was delighted.
The Siddha went to the summit of Meru, abode of the gods, met Urvashi, and told her what the brahmin had said.
She said to that excellent Siddha, "I do not know this brahmin of Kashi; truly, what you tell me has no place in my mind."
Told this, he departed; and after a long time the Siddha went to Varanasi again and was seen once more by the fool.
